# CHAPTER XIII:

THE PERFECTION OF HUMAN SOCIETY (1864)

Minister Adams's success in stopping the rebel rams fixed his position once for all in English society. From that moment he could drop the character of diplomatist, and assume what for an American Minister was an exclusive diplomatic advantage, the character of a kind of American Peer of the Realm. The young man knew no longer what character he bore. Private secretary in the morning, son in the afternoon, young man about town in the evening, the only character he never bore was that of diplomatist. His diplomatic education was at an end; he drifted inevitably into society, and his next education must be one of English social life. He reached his twenty-sixth birthday without the power of earning five dollars in any occupation.

Henry Adams had failed to acquire any useful education; he should at least have acquired social experience. Curiously enough, he failed here also. Every young diplomat felt awkward in an English house from a certainty that they were not precisely wanted there, and a possibility that they might be told so. One morning at breakfast at Bretton in Yorkshire, sitting by Lady Margaret Beaumont, he heard her say to herself in her languid and liberal way, looking into her tea-cup: "I don't think I care for foreigners!"

Horror-stricken, the young man could only execute himself as gaily as he might: "But Lady Margaret, please make one small exception for me!"

Society had no unity; one wandered about in it like a maggot in cheese; it was not a hansom cab, to be got into, or out of, at dinner-time. In seven years he could remember only two functions that seemed to have any meaning for him, and he never knew what that meaning was. One was at Devonshire House, when Mme. de Castiglione, the famous beauty of the Second Empire, entered, and the most refined and aristocratic society in the world instantly formed a lane and stood in ranks to stare at her, while those behind mounted on chairs to look over their neighbors' heads, so that the lady walked through this polite mob, stared completely out of countenance, and fled the house at once. The other was at Stafford House, April 13, 1864, when Garibaldi, in his gray capote over his red shirt, received all London, and three duchesses literally worshipped at his feet. The task of bringing the two into any common relation with an ordered social system was beyond any process yet reached by the education of Henry Adams.

Royalty was in abeyance; the very best society regarded royalty as a bore. Tired of looking on at society from the outside, Adams grew to loathe the sight of his Court dress. Yet Lothrop Motley had said to him early in his apprenticeship that the London dinner and the English country house were the perfection of human society. The young man meditated over it, uncertain of its meaning. Motley could not have meant the cuisine, for there was not then a good cook or a good table in London. He could not have meant the toilettes, which were grotesque, nor manners or taste. Probably he meant that, in his favorite houses, the tone was easy, the talk was good, and the standard of scholarship was high — a small literary class, isolated and lost at the usual London dinner; perfect only in the eyes of a Harvard College historian. They could teach little worth learning, for their tastes were antiquated, and what was altogether fatal for future purposes, they were only English.

A social education in such a medium was bound to be useless in any other, yet Adams had to learn it to the bottom. After five or six years of constant practice, any one can acquire the habit of going from one strange company to another as though silently reflecting that "in a world where we are all insects, no insect is alien"; but the dreamy habit of mind which comes from solitude in crowds is not fitness for social success except in London. England was a social kingdom whose social coinage had no currency elsewhere.

Yet his third season saw him at home in England — more at home there than anywhere else. Close relation in a place like London is a personal mystery as profound as chemical affinity. Thousands pass, and one separates himself from the mass to attach himself to another, and so make, little by little, a group. So it happened, at a Brook Street breakfast in April 1863, that he met a Cambridge undergraduate, Charles Milnes Gaskell, son of the Member for Wenlock, another of the Yorkshire Milneses. Fate had fixed Adams to Yorkshire. More than any other county in England, Yorkshire retained a sort of social independence of London; to a certain degree, evident enough to Yorkshiremen, Yorkshire was not English — or was all England, as they might choose to express it. Mr. Milnes Gaskell was kind, and Mrs. Milnes Gaskell kinder; in England, the family is a serious fact; once admitted to it, one is there for life.

In 1857 Mr. Milnes Gaskell had bought Wenlock Abbey. The Prior's house, a charming specimen of fifteenth-century architecture, had been long left to decay as a farmhouse; she put it in order, and went there in the autumn of 1864. Young Adams was one of her first guests, and drove about Wenlock Edge and the Wrekin with her — ideal repose and rural Shakespearian peace — but a few years of it were likely to complete his education, and fit him to act a fairly useful part in life as an Englishman, an ecclesiastic, and a contemporary of Chaucer.
